# gledach

> Free, installable tools that turn public data into information, insight and
> intelligence. Run them on your own machine. No account to start.
>
> The landing page is signal, slot 01: competitive intelligence your agents can
> query. Ten watchers and one Gmail inbox read what a market publishes, and the
> result is answerable by a machine over MCP. Every other tool has its own page.

gledati (slav.): to watch. What a good analyst does before speaking.

gledach is a shelf, not a platform. The tools published here are written by the
same author but do not share a stack, a codebase or a release cadence, and each
takes whatever shape suits it: a command you type, a dashboard you open, an API
an assistant queries, or just writing. What they share is the promise below.

Look at one before installing it: https://signal.gledach.de is a real signal
deployment exported to one static file, dated and read only. `npm run view` puts
the same dashboard on 127.0.0.1:5180 against your own subject.

## House rules

- Free, and the source is public. MIT unless a dependency makes that impossible.
- Your machine is the runtime. Cloud is for sharing state between machines you own.
- No account to start. Keys, hosted databases and schedules are opt in, later.
- Honest about blind spots. Every tool ships a written audit of what it cannot see.
- Read only until you say otherwise. Paid actions ship disabled, behind a spend ceiling.
- Generated text is labelled as generated. Model output is not verified fact.

## The shelf, in one table

Twelve slots, six filled. What each tool watches, and what it hands back.

| Slot | Tool | Watches | Tells you | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | signal | Ten watchers and one inbox, on whichever market you name | What changed, scored and attributed, over MCP | Live preview |
| 02 | signal-patterns | Nothing. It is the written reasoning | What is watchable, what it costs, how to build it | Docs |
| 03 | whenrun | Day-ahead power prices and renewable share | The cheapest or greenest window, then starts the job in it | Shipped |
| 04 | phonehome | Every DNS query on your own network | Which device talked where, and when that changed | Shipped |
| 05 | recall | Four public registers, against a list of what you own | Which of your things has a notice, and how sure the match is | Shipped |
| 06 | talk | TCP connections owned by local coding agents, on Windows | Which API host, and whether the count is climbing | Shipped |
| 07 | [UNNAMED] | [UNDECIDED] | [UNDECIDED] | Empty |

## Tools

### signal · slot 01 · live preview · the landing page

Situation: you find out a competitor shipped something when a customer mentions
it.

Competitive intelligence your agents can query. Ten watchers and one Gmail inbox
collect what a market publishes, each item is typed and scored and attributed,
patterns several independent publishers corroborate are promoted into
convergences, and the result is exposed over MCP. Ships tracking thirteen AI
coding agents and app builders across two segments. Node, three runtime
dependencies, no build step, libSQL storage that is a local file by default.

It is the only tool on this shelf whose subject is a market the operator names.
whenrun, phonehome and recall watch a power market, a home network, and four
public registers. talk records whichever coding agents are running on the
machine. The landing page is signal for that reason.

- Page: https://gledach.de/
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/signals
- Live preview: https://signal.gledach.de (static export of a real deployment, dated, read only)
- Install guide: https://github.com/gledach/signals/blob/main/docs/start.md
- Agent surface (MCP): https://github.com/gledach/signals/blob/main/docs/mcp.md
- Google Alerts by Gmail: https://github.com/gledach/signals/blob/main/docs/gmail.md
- Blind spots: https://github.com/gledach/signals/blob/main/docs/blindspots.md
- Licence: MIT. Price: 0. Needs Node 22 or newer, and git.

Install:

    git clone https://github.com/gledach/signals && cd signals
    npm install
    npm run db:migrate
    npm run doctor
    npm run view

That runs offline on a fresh clone, on Windows, macOS or Linux. A model key turns
on classification, battlecards and analyst briefs; without one a keyword
classifier runs instead and everything else still works.

The eleven ways in, with what each actually reads:

1. Feeds (`npm run fetch`, every 30 min). Around sixty RSS feeds across the
   roster and the category: Google News, Reddit, vendor blogs, GitHub releases.
   The list derives from the roster, so retargeting rewrites it.
2. Google Alerts by Gmail (`npm run watch:gmail`, local only). Alerts arrive in a
   mailbox, a parser reads them, the result fills a local inbox database. Two
   zones, and the second is easy to forget: nothing reaches the dashboard until
   `email:promote` runs. The refresh token stays on the operator's machine and is
   never shipped to the scheduler.
3. Certificate transparency (`npm run watch:certs`, every 6 h, LEADING). A new
   subdomain gets a certificate before the thing on it is announced.
4. Sitemaps and robots (`npm run watch:sites`, every 6 h, LEADING). Diffed against
   the last snapshot; new paths, removed paths and rule changes.
5. Hacker News (`npm run watch:hn`, daily) via the Algolia search API, with
   points, comments, author and timestamps as structured fields.
6. GitHub (`npm run watch:github`, daily). Releases, breaking-change tags and
   issue complaints. 60 requests an hour unauthenticated, 5,000 with a token.
7. YouTube captions (`npm run watch:youtube`, daily) over HTTP, no audio download
   and no transcription, free for roughly four videos in five.
8. Answer-engine visibility (`npm run watch:aeo`, weekly). Which brands each
   engine names when a buyer forms a shortlist. Detection is a deterministic
   word-boundary match, not a model judging model output.
9. Model routing (`npm run watch:routing`, daily, LEADING). A public, openly
   licensed data API: which models the market routes tokens to. Only movement past
   a threshold is emitted, so a flat week is silent.
10. Search discovery (`npm run watch:tavily`, daily). Two queries per company,
    budget guarded against a free monthly tier with a cooldown.
11. Search interest (`npm run watch:trends`, weekly over 4 passes). Batched to the
    eight stalest queries per run, because the upstream limiter refuses thirty two
    in a row.

What happens to one item: classify (Haiku, or a free keyword classifier with no
key, and the method is recorded on the row), score 0 to 100 re-weighted for this
job rather than for news, store one row keyed on a hash of its own content so
every write is idempotent, correlate into convergences by theme and count rules
with a structured citation graph back to the evidence, then synthesise.
Battlecards come from Sonnet, deep research from Opus across a 180-day window,
five analyst modes from a written persona, and a weekly report that uses no model
at all because its arithmetic is deterministic.

The dashboard has three views worth naming, and the landing page carries a real
capture of each. Live Feed is not a list of headlines: a convergence is the unit,
scored from its own evidence, with the rule that fired it stated on the row.
Compare sets one company as the anchor against up to three rivals across
positioning, segment, pricing, strengths and weaknesses, and marks a cell
`[unverified]` where the collected evidence does not support the claim. Battle is
call prep for one competitor, ranking the strongest points and the objections to
expect against the deal in front of you, and it is labelled as generated text.

What the tool leaves behind is the point: every pass appends to a local libSQL
database rather than refreshing a feed, so after a few weeks you are querying
months of attributed, scored, deduplicated history rather than reading today's
news. Three ways to use it. Ask an agent, through eight MCP tools
(list_companies, search_signals, get_convergences, get_battlecard, list_briefs,
get_brief, run_analyst, market_summary) plus signal:// resources, so an MCP
client answers from your collected history instead of from training data. Search
it yourself, in plain SQL with no ORM and no schema-deploy step, or over the JSON
endpoints, or with `npm run transcripts -- --stats` for word counts per
competitor across archived YouTube transcripts and `npm run transcripts --
"pricing"` to find every mention with snippets. Or compare week to week with
`npm run report:weekly`, a deterministic snapshot per ISO week that uses no model
and is idempotent, so a missed week can be backfilled.

What is actually retained: attributed signals with a link back to source (2,600+
in the deployment behind the preview), excerpts of YouTube transcripts rather
than whole videos, weekly report snapshots, generated briefs and battlecards, the
per-call model cost ledger, and each watcher's own baseline, which is what lets a
new subdomain be reported as new rather than merely present. It is not a copy of
the web. Every row is keyed by a hash of its own content, so re-running a pass
collapses duplicates rather than growing the file.

There is also a localhost dashboard with eight views, and an experimental Chrome
side panel that is not covered by the test gate.

Every signal-reporting MCP tool returns a coverage block: a status of fresh,
slowing, stale or never, plus a trustEmptyResult flag. Without it, a watcher that
quietly stopped running reads to an agent as a calm market.

Read only by default and not merely by convention: run_analyst is the only tool
that spends money and it ships with permission withheld. Opting in binds it to a
rolling 24-hour ceiling shared with the scheduler and the CLI.

Setting it up, for a reader who is not a developer: three commands put it on a
laptop with a real example dataset already loaded, and the only thing you then
change is who it watches. Requirements are a Mac, a Windows PC or a Linux
machine, and Node 22. No account, no card, and nothing collected leaves the
machine. The install guide assumes no prior terminal experience and takes about
fifteen minutes; with experience it is closer to two.

Pointing it at your own market is one file. `cp
config/companies.default.mjs config/companies.local.mjs`, then write one block
per competitor:

    export const companies = {
      acme: {
        id: 'acme', name: 'Acme', domain: 'acme.com',
        query: '"Acme Corp" OR "acme.com"',
        repos: ['acme/platform'],
        subreddits: ['acme'],
      },
    };

The field worth thought is `query`, because a company name is often an ordinary
word: "Cursor" is also the thing blinking in a text box, so the query is written
to catch the company and not the word. The shipped file carries thirteen worked
examples, each with a note on what it collides with. Everything else rebuilds
itself from that list: the feeds, the searches, the repositories checked and the
dashboard's own labels. There is no second place to keep in sync.

Three reassurances, all mechanical rather than promised. Your file sits beside
the shipped example rather than replacing it, so pulling a new version never
overwrites what you wrote and never produces a merge conflict. `npm test` fails
if any of the thirteen shipped brand names is still present anywhere outside
`config/`, or if the dashboard's labels have drifted from your list, so the
example market cannot be left behind by accident. And collecting is free: a
model key turns on classification, battlecards and briefs, and without one a
keyword classifier runs instead while everything else works the same.

Under the hood this is six configuration layers, each resolving as an
environment variable, then a gitignored `.local.mjs`, then the shipped
`.default.mjs`: the roster, the feeds, the deal-context axes, subdomain scoring,
the agent policy and the answer-engine prompts. Most deployments only ever edit
the first.

Figures: 11 collection surfaces, ~60 RSS feeds, 13 companies across 2 segments,
8 MCP tools, 3 runtime dependencies, 2,600+ signals stored in the deployment
behind the preview, 15 smoke sections and 5 fixture suites in the offline gate,
and about $15 to $25 a month at the shipped models and cadence. Cadence moves
that last figure far more than model choice: a per-company job on a six-hourly
tier costs four times a daily one for no added freshness, a mistake that cost this
deployment around $209 a month before it was caught.

### signal-patterns · slot 02 · reference

Situation: you want to build one of these, and the hard part is knowing what is
watchable at all.

How to build tools that watch the public web and feed the result to an agent.
Not a framework: there is no package to install and nothing to version, because
the reasoning is the reusable part and the code around it usually is not. The
reference implementation is signal.

- Page: https://gledach.de/signal-patterns
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/signal-patterns
- What is watchable: https://github.com/gledach/signal-patterns/blob/main/sources.md
- What it costs: https://github.com/gledach/signal-patterns/blob/main/techniques.md
- Building a watcher: https://github.com/gledach/signal-patterns/blob/main/building-a-watcher.md
- Being consumable by agents: https://github.com/gledach/signal-patterns/blob/main/agent-integration.md

Thesis: a company is only as visible as what it exposes publicly, and the useful
signals are the ones it exposes before it means to. Ordered by lead time:
infrastructure (weeks), hiring (months, vague), documentation (hours), changelog
(hours), marketing (at launch), press (after). Certificate logs run 20 to 30 days
ahead; changelog pages change on 73% of monitors within 90 days.

Eight patterns, each extracted from a bug that shipped: store chokepoint;
canonical and mirror; never store an uncomputed verdict; read-only agent surface;
the coverage block; zone separation; assertions as guardrails; collect rather
than write. The bias throughout is that an AI pipeline fails silently and
pleasantly, so most of these are machinery for turning a quiet failure into a
loud one.

The shortest version: watch what leaks rather than what is announced; cadence is
the cost dial, not model choice; batch and cache before optimising anything else;
a failed model writes nothing; return "I do not know" as data; agents read by
default and permission must not scale with capability; a skill is a supply chain
(341 malicious skills among roughly 13,000 in one 2026 marketplace audit); and
every rule above needs an assertion or it is a comment.

### whenrun · slot 03 · shipped

Situation: power can cost three times more in the evening than it does at midday,
and a backup job does not care when it runs.

Run it when the power is cheap. Watches day-ahead electricity prices and the
renewable-share forecast, finds the cheapest or greenest window that still meets
a job's deadline, and starts the job there. The first tool on this shelf that acts
on what it sees rather than reporting it, and the only one with nothing at all to
install.

- Page: https://gledach.de/whenrun
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/whenrun
- Running it for real: https://github.com/gledach/whenrun/blob/main/docs/running-it.md
- What it cannot do: https://github.com/gledach/whenrun/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md
- Licence: MIT. Price: 0. Needs Node 22 or newer.

Install:

    git clone https://github.com/gledach/whenrun && cd whenrun
    node bin/whenrun.mjs prices
    node bin/whenrun.mjs where

There is no `npm install`, because there is nothing to install.

Commands: prices, plan, run, daemon, report, where, doctor. Three objectives:
cheapest minimises price, greenest maximises renewable share, balanced blends the
two. A job marked interruptible may be scattered across non-adjacent slots;
otherwise it gets one unbroken block. The task is told what it was scheduled into
through WHENRUN_WINDOW_START, WHENRUN_WINDOW_END, WHENRUN_SPOT_EUR_MWH,
WHENRUN_RENEWABLE_PCT and WHENRUN_SLOTS.

Safety, because it runs commands unattended: the command comes from your task
file and never from a price feed, an argument or the network, and there is no
code path that builds a command out of fetched data; two independent locks, since
a task needs `enabled: true` and the command needs `--execute`; it refuses rather
than guesses on stale data, an impossible deadline or a window that closed while
the daemon slept; and the MCP server is read only, so an agent can ask when power
is cheap but cannot start anything.

Data: two keyless sources. Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE) at 15-minute resolution
for DE-LU, AT, FR, NL and more, and aWATTar at 60 minutes for DE and AT. Price
data is CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur and SMARD.de via Energy-Charts. `doctor`
cross-checks the two and warns when they disagree by more than a rounding error.
Verified against live data for DE-LU, AT, FR, CH, NL, ES and PL. Ships set to
postcode 82319 Starnberg in DE-LU.

Agent surface: six read-only MCP tools (get_prices, cheapest_window,
greenest_window, list_tasks, plan_task, savings_report), each result carrying a
coverage block and a trustEmptyResult flag.

Figures: 2 keyless price sources, 7 zones verified live, 0 runtime dependencies,
128 offline tests. Savings are reported against the delivered bill as well as the
spot price and both are labelled, because only the energy component moves by the
hour; `report` also prints the standing charge for the period, since no amount of
load shifting changes it.

Blind spots: your actual tariff (it uses the numbers in your tariff file, and
doctor warns while you are on the shipped defaults); whether you are on a dynamic
tariff at all; your own generation, which is not modelled; grid fees that vary by
time, modelled as flat; whether your job really draws the kW you declared; and it
cannot pause a running command, so honouring an interruptible split is your
script's job.

### phonehome · slot 04 · shipped

Situation: nothing on a home network tells you where it has been sending data, or
when that changed.

See what your devices talk to. A local DNS resolver that records which domains
every device on your network contacts, classifies them, and says when one starts
talking somewhere new. It does not block and it does not upload: finding out is a
different job from filtering. Reads existing Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, dnsmasq or
Unbound logs, so months of history are available without re-pointing a network.

- Page: https://gledach.de/phonehome
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/phonehome
- What it cannot do: https://github.com/gledach/phonehome/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md
- Licence: MIT. Price: 0. Needs Node 22 or newer.

Install:

    git clone https://github.com/gledach/phonehome && cd phonehome
    node bin/phonehome.mjs import /var/log/pihole.log --execute
    node bin/phonehome.mjs report
    node bin/phonehome.mjs new

Commands: watch, report, new, devices, import, doctor. `new` is the one that earns
its keep: a steady list of domains is background noise, but a doorbell contacting
something at 03:00 that it has never contacted before is worth knowing.

The resolver binds 127.0.0.1:5335 by default, which only the local machine can
use, deliberately: serving a whole house is a decision you make rather than
something that happens because you tried the tool. `--host=0.0.0.0` plus a router
DHCP change covers every device. Port 53 needs privileges on most systems.

Safety: it never modifies a response, forwarding packets and returning the
upstream answer unchanged, so it cannot break name resolution by inventing one;
the only packet it ever composes is a SERVFAIL when the upstream is unreachable.
It never blocks anything, and the default upstream is whatever the machine was
already using.

Agent surface: five read-only MCP tools (list_devices, get_report, new_contacts,
classify_domain, blind_spots). Every result carries the blind-spot list and a
trustEmptyResult flag, so an agent cannot report a clean bill of health the data
does not support.

Figures: 4 log formats read and detected automatically, 0 runtime dependencies,
64 offline tests. "unknown" is kept visible and counted rather than guessed at,
and the share of traffic using encrypted DNS is reported because that traffic
routes around the tool entirely.

Blind spots: encrypted DNS, since a device using DoH or DoT never asks this
resolver anything and becomes completely invisible, though `watch` flags the
moment a device looks up a known DoH endpoint; content, because this reads the
question in a DNS packet and nothing else, and a domain being contacted is not
the same as data being sent; devices with hardcoded resolvers, which only a
firewall rule catches; who as opposed to what, since it sees devices and not
people; and classification coverage, which is why every report prints the
unknown share.

### recall · slot 05 · shipped

Situation: the notice for the thing in your kitchen was published, and nobody
sent it to you.

Tell me when something I own is recalled. Keeps a list of the things one person
owns and checks it against four public registers, none of which needs an account.

- Page: https://gledach.de/recall
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/recall
- What it cannot do: https://github.com/gledach/recall/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md
- Licence: MIT. Price: 0. Needs Node 22 or newer.

Install:

    git clone https://github.com/gledach/recall && cd recall
    npm test
    cp config/inventory.default.mjs config/inventory.local.mjs
    node bin/recall.mjs check

Registers: EU Safety Gate (consumer products, toys, appliances, electronics,
vehicles, EU scope); BfArM (German medicine supply shortages, which is
availability rather than safety, and every notice from that source carries that
sentence with it); NHTSA (US vehicle safety campaigns); endoflife.date (software
past its security support date, every jurisdiction). Safety Gate has no
documented API but publishes a weekly XML report export, and a report reference
is a stable cursor, so a refresh only fetches weeks it has not seen and a
published week never changes so its cache never expires.

Five inventory kinds with the fields each needs before it can be checked at all:
appliance and device need make and model and also accept a barcode; vehicle needs
make, model and year and also accepts a VIN; software needs an endoflife.date
product slug and also accepts a cycle; medicine needs a name and also accepts a
PZN. A missing required field is a startup error, not a skipped entry, because an
entry silently ignored looks exactly like an entry with nothing wrong.

Matches are graded rather than binary: exact when a barcode, PZN or VIN matched
or the register matched it for us; strong when make and model both appear in the
notice; weak when a distinctive model number appears but the make does not;
mention when only the make appears, which is almost always noise and hidden
unless asked for. Weak is shown by default, because missing the one that mattered
is worse and invisible while a false alarm is merely annoying. Nothing in the
output ever says "you are affected": it says what matched and how.

Add the barcode where the box still has one. Roughly half the EU alerts carry
one and every German shortage report carries a PZN. Only add digits readable off
the thing itself, because a wrong barcode is worse than no barcode: it will match
something unrelated and be reported as certain.

Agent surface: five read-only MCP tools (check_inventory, list_inventory,
notice_history, describe_sources, blind_spots). Read only on purpose: it cannot
add to an inventory and it cannot acknowledge a notice, because acknowledging is
a person deciding they have dealt with something. Every result carries its
coverage and the confidence grade of each match, because a model asked "is my car
recalled?" will otherwise turn "no notices found" into "your car is fine".

Figures: 4 registers, 0 keys, 0 runtime dependencies including its own CSV and
XML readers, 98 offline tests.

Blind spots: no UK, Swiss, Australian, Canadian or Japanese register; German
vehicle recalls are not checked because that register sits behind a proof-of-work
challenge; medicine coverage is German shortages only; registers publish days to
weeks after a decision; matching is text against text; and it checks your list,
not your house. A source that is unreachable is reported as unreachable, never as
clean. "Nothing found" and "could not look" must never render the same way, which
is the single most important thing in the codebase.

This is not legal, medical or safety advice. If a notice concerns you, go to the
register's own page and read the original.

### talk · slot 06 · shipped

Situation: a long coding-agent session opens connections and never closes them.
When the Windows client port range fills, other programs fail in about 20
milliseconds, and it looks like the network died.

Which API hosts your local coding agents connect to. Samples TCP connections on
Windows, follows each process up to its parent, and reads the certificate name
of a new public host once. A Node helper under Cursor counts as Cursor. The URL
path stays encrypted. Prompts and Authorization headers are never stored. Zero
runtime dependencies, and the sampler ships inside the clone.

- Page: https://gledach.de/talk
- Repository: https://github.com/gledach/talk
- What it cannot see: https://github.com/gledach/talk#what-it-cannot-see
- Licence: MIT. Price: 0. Needs Node 22 or newer, and Windows for a sample.

Install:

    git clone https://github.com/gledach/talk && cd talk
    node bin/talk.mjs once
    node bin/talk.mjs watch
    node bin/talk.mjs doctor

There is no `npm install`, because there is nothing to install. The sampler is
core/win-snapshot.ps1, in the repository. Logs go to data/, which is gitignored.

Commands, always as node bin/talk.mjs, never as a bare talk command: once,
watch, report, doctor. watch stays in the terminal. It does not
install a Windows service or a scheduled task. The name talk is already an
npm package and a Unix program, so this tool does not install a talk command. A line is written when a process
holds 500 connections or more, when an agent's count climbs by 30 in one
interval, when orphaned sockets grow, or when an agent asks for a host it has
not used before.

It does not close sockets and it does not restart anything. Restarting the agent
releases sockets it still owns. Orphans from a dead process stay until reboot or
an admin restart of winnat.

One real sample, 2026-10-24: 13,380 TCP connections, 3,647 of them orphaned. A
Cursor helper held 9,113 to us4p.cursorvm.com and us3p.cursorvm.com. A process
that had already exited still held 3,591 to us3p.cursorvm.com, and could no
longer be named. The default client port range on Windows is 16,384.

Agents it tags: Cursor, Claude, Grok, Codex, Windsurf, Aider, and a child whose
parent is one of them. VS Code uses the same Node helper subtype and is not
tagged on that fact alone.

Figures: 0 runtime dependencies, 0 accounts, 4 certificate reads per sample by
default, spent on the busiest agent first.

Blind spots: a hostname that was never sent in the TLS handshake, because the
certificate read connects to the IP and a server that requires the right
hostname comes back blank; the path after the host, which stays encrypted; an
agent that resolves names through its own encrypted DNS and never presents a
certificate name; a process that exited before the first sample, whose sockets
still count but whose owner can no longer be named; anything that is not TCP;
any operating system other than Windows, where report can print a log you
already have and once and watch cannot take a sample.

### Slot 07 · not built

Empty. The shelf is built to hold a dozen. Nothing is planned publicly, and there
is no roadmap to quote.

Requests go to https://github.com/gledach/requests, a public queue. The form asks
the three questions that decide whether a thing is watchable at all: what you
check by hand and how often, where it is published, and whether seeing it needs an
account. There is no request address: a request sent privately is invisible to
everyone else and cannot be labelled or linked, so the public queue is the only
channel and therefore the whole list. A request that would help more people than the person asking
is built first, and the open issues are how you check that.

## Previews

Explained in full at https://gledach.de/about#previews, which is where this
lives on the site: it describes a deployment convention, which matters to
someone deciding whether to trust a preview and not to someone who just wants
the tool.

Convention: `<tool>.gledach.de`. One per tool, replaced in place. A preview is a
static export of a real deployment: real data, dated, read only. The export asks
the running viewer the same questions a browser asks and inlines the answers, so
it cannot drift from the thing it was taken from. A re-export overwrites it, so a
preview is the most recent snapshot rather than an archive.
